name: structural
title: Structural tells
description: Rhetorical shapes rather than phrases, distilled from the replies to Simon Willison's thread and from sloptells' structural descriptions. These survive rewording, which is what makes them worth a rule. Two of the four shapes people named turned out not to be expressible here at all; the research log says which and why.

rules.name: Hedge, then affirm
rules.description: The concession that costs nothing: “It's not perfect, but it works.” A weakness is admitted in a subordinate clause and immediately overridden, so the reader gets the feeling of balance without any of the information.
rules.suggest: Say what is wrong with it, and how much that matters. If the answer is “not much”, drop the first half.

hit: It's not perfect, but it works.
This isn't elegant, but it does the job.
It was not cheap, but the team shipped on time.
miss: It is not the answer we wanted.
It's not a bug but a feature.

rules.name: Asking yourself an easy question
rules.description: The self-interview: “Is it perfect? No. Does it work? Yes.” A question nobody asked, answered in one word, twice in a row.
rules.suggest: State the answer. The question was never in doubt or you would not have written it.

hit: Is it perfect? No. But it ships.
Does this scale? Not really. We are fine with that.
Should you use it? Yes, if you already run Postgres.
miss: Is it perfect? Depends who you ask.
Does this scale? The benchmark says forty thousand a second.
